#963. Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe

It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points

José Mourinho had already done the por qué?, the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists.

He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out.

“We have the best goalkeeper in the world, but none of us cried because Thibaut couldn’t play,” Mourinho said. Plenty might have felt like it, more reason to be fearful. But the coach called Andriy Lunin, the substitute goalkeeper so serious that he bought a roll of artificial turf and spent the pandemic diving round the living room of his flat, and told him this was his moment: “You train to play, not to sit on the bench, so go on.” As for the rest of them, the manager told them nothing changes: the plan remains in place. By the time they headed back to the dressing room, “Fucking get in!” echoing along the Camp Nou corridor, so it had proved.

Thirteen years later, Mourinho was back in Barcelona for a clásico and he had guided Madrid to a 2-1 win. It wasn’t supposed to be like this, or maybe it was. Barcelona, the team who had won nine in a row, banging in 4.3 goals per game, had been beaten by Madrid, the team who had lost twice already and, truth be told, were mostly just not very good. The night it could have been all over, the title race done when it’s not even in November, was instead the night it finally started. “If you leave here nine points behind, it’s very heavy psychologically; if it’s six, it’s more balanced; if it’s three, that’s different,” Mourinho said.

This was different, and so is the season now. Counting the clásicos all those years ago, Mourinho racked up his sixth consecutive meeting with Barcelona without defeat, and there had been no parked bus, nor many lumps kicked. They didn’t just desperately hang on, although there was a moment when Dean Huijsen saved a shot with his face. Nor had they just waited for a moment, resisting and then robbing it, even if João Cancelo did insist: “That’s Madrid; they don’t have many chances but they score them.” The final shot count said 18-10 to Barcelona, and possession was 62% Barcelona’s.

“The way we won is important: you can win luckily or by defending a lot. But we won with calmness and totally deservedly. We did it by being organised, concentrated and having the courage to come out from the back,” Mourinho said. And if that might have been pushing it a little – and, let’s face it, the analyses might be different had Lunin not made an astonishing save from Gerard Martín or Lamine Yamal’s second-half shot not faded just past the post – he had a point.

Barcelona were not at their best. They had been hurried and imprecise, Rodri telling his teammates to lower their “pulse rate” as they came out for the second half. Lamine Yamal somehow missed an extraordinary chance just before the break. And when they did tighten the screw in the second half, they couldn’t break the wall. Xavi Espart was forced off, yet another injury at the back, the failure to sign a centre-back in the spotlight again. Yet this was still a faster, more aggressive, tighter Madrid than anyone expected. Asked to define it, Lunin went for “discipline and attitude”. And if that is partly about occasion, the least you can ask for, it’s more than you sometimes get.

Besides, it was also more than that. More than Marc Cucurella getting under Lamine Yamal’s skin, although he certainly succeeded. They went for the space beyond Barcelona’s full-backs: superb in his first clásico, aged 19, Yan Diomandé – the left winger – got more touches than any Madrid player, and protected his full-back as well. But it was more than that, too. More than the wonderful winning goal, a flash of inspiration with Jude Bellingham going all Nureyev, the ball flitting between his feet and Gabriel Jesus’s legs, pirouetting to release Eduardo Camavinga. This was a team with an idea and a victory that vindicated their manager, some kind of resurrection.

Before the game, Rodri said that one of Madrid’s tricks is to convince you that they’re not that good, but insisted he wouldn’t fall into that trap. Still he felt that plan particularly. Pedri did too. Bellingham dealt with Rodri, Bernardo Silva with Pedri. Pressed and tired too, according to Hansi Flick, neither truly took control. The inclusion of Arda Güler and Silva – the surprise in the middle, starting his first league game in six weeks – underlined an intention for Madrid to keep the ball when they could. They actually had a midfield, which was new. From the back they tried to build, draw Barcelona in. And if a time came when they had to wait, to put bodies in before the ball, well, they would do that too. Six times Barcelona shots were blocked. At least twice more, shots were taken from their toes. At the other end, meanwhile, Madrid attacked with an intent and an incision that probably drew the clearer chances: the xG showed 1.19 v 1.94.

Alaves 1-1 Malaga, Rayo Vallecano 0-3 Elche, Racing Santander 2-1 Espanyol, Valencia 1-2 Villarreal, Atlético 1-0 Deportiva A Coruna, A Bilbao 4-0 Getafe, Celta Vigo 0-0 Real Betis, Real Sociedad 2-1 Levante, Barcelona 1-2 Real Madrid

Victory puts Madrid three points behind Barcelona and, Federico Valverde claimed, “will give us a kickstart”. It has taken 10 weeks but it’s game on. Hay liga, as they like to say. There is league. There is Madrid, too. Something has shifted, starting in Rome, where 70 dreadful minutes gave way to 20 pretty good ones, another inexplicable comeback actually having something of an explanation, too. The changes were impossible to ignore. Valverde and Aurélien Tchouaméni no longer the partnership in the middle, Valverde going to right-back instead. Güler playing. Diomandé playing. And, yes, Vinícius Júnior not playing. “I’m not stubborn; I can change,” Mourinho said. Madrid have won five in succession now; something was seen that night, a way ahead. They’ve won every game since Vinícius was suspended, facile and perhaps even cruel though that may be to say. And since Mourinho grew a beard, if you believe in that kind of thing.

Before the clásico, Mourinho had said it wasn’t fair to compare his team, a side in construction and a long way from the finished product, to Barcelona. He insisted that he was still getting to know his players; he hadn’t been there long, after all. After the clásico, he admitted: “We have improved, we can’t hide that.” The idea has shifted, almost like it was an epiphany: “I’ve learned something about the middle of the pitch; I have learned that a mixture is better, that it is better to have a combination of qualities than two players of similar characteristics.” In short, Tchouaméni and Valverde doesn’t work. There needs to be some football in there somewhere, and so a shift started. Sunday came as a kind of confirmation, a hope, an identity emerging.

“The best Madrid is born at the Camp Nou,” ran the headline in El País. “Madrid are here now,” AS’s cover said. “I won’t let them have their heads on the moon; if we win this and then don’t win at the Sardinero, it won’t mean much,” Mourinho said, but this was a start, not just an end in itself. At full time, Mourinho headed on to the pitch and shook Lunin’s hand as all around players embraced. High in the north-east corner, Madrid’s fans stayed and sang. Back home, Courtois was watching. He had “a horrible night” on Saturday, they said, but now he was feeling a little better. They all were.

#959. World Cup 2034: Does Saudi Arabia shelving Neom Stadium spell trouble?

Since winning the right to hold the 2034 World Cup unopposed, Saudi Arabia has been pulling away from sport. With reports that its most ambitious stadium project will be abandoned, what does this mean for the World Cup?

It was billed as "the most unique stadium in the world," a key pillar of Saudi Arabia's World Cup 2034 plans. But now Neom Stadium, part of the kingdom's ambitious aims to build a 170-kilometer-long (111-mile) city in the desert known as The Line, looks set to be scrapped, with the broader project scaled back significantly.

A recent Reuters report said the stadium, which according to the country's bid book was going to be "350 meters (1,148 feet) above ground" and have "stunning vistas, and a roof created from the city itself," would no longer be built for the tournament, where it was to host a quarterfinal and several other games.

Observers of the gulf country saw this coming.

"When I was in Saudi Arabia in December there were already plenty of signals that the whole Neom project was being put on the back burner, if not abandoned altogether," F. Gregory Gause III, a regional expert from the Middle East Institute think tank in Washington D.C., told DW.

"I see it as part of a general reevaluation of their fiscal situation, both in light of the oil market before the current war and in light of the damage that the war is doing. The drawback from sports commitments is just part of a more general reassessment of priorities in the current, more straitened, situation."

Saudi Arabia's sports splurge that saw players like Cristiano Ronaldo join the country's football league and the kingdom invest in all sorts of sports in myriad ways has slowed dramatically. The country pulled funding for the multibillion dollar LIV Golf as well as events in snooker, tennis and rugby and also withdrew from ambitious plans to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games in Neom.

Sports had formed a key part of Saudi Arabia's Project 2030, which aimed to diversify the country's economy away from oil and increase its soft power. But Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the governor of the Saudi-government operated Public Investment Fund (PIF), which also owns Premier League football club Newcastle United, said earlier this year that the PIF was "reassessing its priorities" amid war in the region.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The impact of the war has not only made the economic rationalization more important, but it's also accelerated the desire to rethink some of these projects in the sense that Neom is now being repurposed as an industrial center on the Red Sea, which has obviously assumed much greater urgency since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blocked," Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, author of "Kingdom of Football: Saudi Arabia and the Remaking of World Soccer," told DW.

There are, Coates Ulrichsen continued, clear parallels with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where plans to build 12 stadiums resulted in only eight being used at the tournament. The Arab Spring uprising arrived shortly after the bid was accepted by FIFA and, though it didn't impact the country directly, it destabilized the region both politically and economically.

Neither Saudi Arabia's World Cup organizing authority or Sports Ministry has responded to questions from DW about whether we may again see fewer stadiums than the planned 15 for the 2034 World Cup, which could feature 64 teams.

"We're seeing the same obviously with Saudi Arabia now," said Coates Ulrichsen, who is also a fellow for the Middle East at Rice University in the US.

"[FIFA President] Gianni Infantino announced Saudi would be the only bidder on the 4th of October 2023. Three days later was October 7th, so within three days, the region was effectively in flames," he said.

Since then, there has been the Israel-US war against Iran, while Houthi attacks continue to hit Saudi Arabia as part of the conflict in Yemen, meaning that: "This whole hosting cycle is taking place against a backdrop of considerable uncertainty and kind of real tension."

But though the scope and cost of it may be reduced, Saudi Arabia's softening commitment to sport will not likely apply so firmly to the biggest sporting event in the world, said Gause.

"I think it continues to be a major priority, because of its global importance and because the Saudis will want to do at least as well, if not outshine, Qatar's hosting earlier."

Relations between Saudi Arabia and Qatar have improved since an agreement in 2021 but the pair remain regional rivals, something Coates Ulrichsen agrees will spur the 2034 hosts on.

As such, the 2034 tournament will still likely be a high-end affair, with Saudi Arabia building most stadiums from scratch. But, said Coates Ulrichsen, it may look somewhat different to what was planned.

"The fact that at least the Saudis were able to host a big event with 60,000 people in the stadiums, full stadiums without any security concerns [the Gulf Cup football final which they won this week] is a good sign," he said.

The regional expert thinks more matches could end up being hosted in the two biggest Saudi cities, Riyadh and Jeddah. This may be at the expense of some venues nearer the east coast such as Al Khobar or Al Ahsa. These are separated from Iran by the Persian Gulf, which includes the Strait of Hormuz, and could be reconsidered depending on the state of political affairs.

Saudi Arabia host football's Asian Cup in January, which Coates Ulrichsen thinks will be an "early test of whether that is viable to have a weeks-long major tournament under these conditions."

With nearly eight years until the World Cup, the political and economic situation in the country is difficult to predict. While the supposed shelving of Neom Stadium and general Saudi sporting withdrawal poses questions of commitment more broadly, it appears the World Cup show will go on. But probably not quite as billed.

#957. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

#956. Iranian scientists in the United States face major upheaval

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sophia Chen is a freelance writer in Ohio.

A destroyed police building in Tehran, where the conflict in Iran has severely disrupted the lives of citizens, including students at home and abroad.Credit: Majid Saeedi/Getty

Babak wants to finish his PhD in 2028. He started his programme in 2024 at a university in the south of the United States. To stay on track, in July this year, he began writing the first paper on his health-care-related research. Between reading papers and coding, his attention wanders.

“I have to check the news to see if my country has been bombarded or not,” says Babak, who is from Iran. He and many of the researchers interviewed by Nature’s careers team for this article are using pseudonyms out of concern for their own safety and that of their families, as well as fears of potential career repercussions.

Life in the past year has been tumultuous for the people of Iran. The country has been engulfed in violence inflicted both by foreign nations and by its own government. The events have turned the lives of many Iranian students and early-career researchers upside down, both in Iran itself and in other countries — particularly the United States, where people from Iran have also faced restrictions on travel, visas and work. Nearly 12,000 Iranian postgraduate students were training in the United States during the 2024–25 academic year, according to Open Doors, an annual report published by the Institute of International Education in New York City.

In June 2025, Israel bombed nuclear and military facilities in Iran, and Iran retaliated with missile and drone attacks in Israel, resulting in what is now referred to as the 12-day war. The United States also joined the conflict, carrying out strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. The following December and January, an economic crisis in Iran — during which inflation hit 42% — sparked nationwide protests. In quashing these demonstrations, Iran’s government killed as many as 30,000 of its citizens, according to an estimate cited by The Guardian newspaper.

And in February, the United States and Israel attacked Iran over its nuclear-weapons programme in an ongoing conflict that has killed an estimated 20,000 people, both military and civilian, across all nations involved, according to Iran War Live, an independent open-source intelligence platform. One student told Nature that members of her family had had to leave their home in a city owing to bombardment and seek refuge in a village with some of their relatives. The Iranian government shut off the country’s Internet for nearly three months between February and May. During that time, Iranian researchers in other countries could not communicate consistently with loved ones in Iran.

Changes to US immigration policy upended the lives of Iranian researchers further. In June 2025, the administration of US President Donald Trump issued a travel ban that barred people from 12 countries, including Iran, from entering the United States, subject to limited exceptions and case-by-case waivers. According to the presidential proclamation, Iran was included because it “is a state sponsor of terrorism”.

‘Heartbreaking’: Iranian scientists on losing labs, libraries and liberty

‘Heartbreaking’: Iranian scientists on losing labs, libraries and liberty

Furthermore, in December 2025 and January 2026, two executive agency memos, citing reasons of national security, forced many Iranian researchers already in the United States into limbo over their immigration status. Together, the memos expanded the travel ban to 39 countries and effectively froze the processing of all applications from those countries, including those for student visas, permanent residency (also known as a green card) and work authorization.

During that period, which stretched until June, the federal government would neither approve nor deny applications for work authorization or changes in legal status. This meant that people from those 39 countries were trapped in a bureaucratic limbo. For Iranian researchers in the United States, uncertainty about their career pathways, compounded with stress about loved ones in Iran, left many feeling a profound lack of agency over their future.

The researchers who spoke to Nature wanted to raise awareness of their situation among the academic community. But even offering their stories anonymously felt risky to many of them. Several expressed the fear of repercussions from the Iranian and US governments.

In what would turn out to be a horribly timed visit to see his family, Nima, a PhD student in health care in the southern United States, travelled to Iran in May 2025. Nima planned to be there for only two weeks, and to then return to the United States to marry his fiancée, who is also from Iran. He decided to visit because his mother was ill, and his father had told him they missed him. It was a risky choice, because although he had legal status to study in the United States, his visa — required for entry back into the country — had expired. He planned to apply for a new visa during his visit to Iran.

After the June 2025 travel ban, Nima could not return to the United States. He became distraught. “Every day I cried,” he says, speaking a year later from Iran. He was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for two weeks. In August, he had to resign from his PhD, because his university limits a student’s leave of absence to two academic semesters. Even now, he has told few friends in Iran that he is back. “I think they will think I am a loser,” he says. Returning to Iran to see his family, he says, was “the worst decision of my life”.

During the Internet blackout, he texted with his fiancée every day using a VPN. They used voice or video calls rarely, because he would become too emotional. He was accepted into a health-care-related master’s programme in another country, but that country’s government did not grant him a visa in time to start the school year in September. He does not know when he will see his fiancée again.

It wasn’t just the travel ban that upended lives. The pause on approving applications — as a result of the government memos — between December 2025 and June 2026 threw into disarray the lives of many Iranian students in the United States. One PhD student described feeling so burnt out that he often could not bear to leave his house. “You don’t know if you will have a job, or if you need to move to another country,” he says.

Several students say that the pause didn’t make sense to them. The United States has spent money training Iranian students, but it seemed that “they don’t want to take advantage of what they’ve invested in”, one PhD student says.

The policy supports the Trump administration’s efforts to reduce immigration — including by international students — according to Kevan Harris, a sociologist at the University of California, Los Angeles, who studies Iranian politics. “The government increases the burden on people, and then some people just say, ‘Screw this, I’m leaving,’” says Harris.

International PhD students to face strict limits on time in the US

International PhD students to face strict limits on time in the US

Azin, who earned a PhD from a university in the midwestern United States in December 2025, could not work because of the pause. Shortly after graduation, an engineering company in the United States wanted to hire her, but dropped the offer because she lacked work authorization, she says. A postdoc opportunity fell through for the same reason. She had applied for Optional Practical Training, a work authorization offered for up to three years to students who have completed a degree in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) subjects, but the pause froze that application as well.

She sold most of her possessions and did not have a permanent home or an income after she graduated. For half a year, she travelled around Illinois, Alabama, Missouri, North Carolina and Minnesota, staying with friends and family members for a few weeks at a time.

Nature reached out to the Trump administration to respond to these comments on the pause. A spokesperson for the Department of State said that the memos were issued to “protect the national security, public safety, and national interests of the United States and its people”.

“As the Secretary of State has said repeatedly, a visa is a privilege, not a right,” the spokesperson said. The department adjudicates each visa application on a case-by-case basis, they added.

Michael Carrick's struggles mean Manchester United are expected to soon be looking for their ninth manager of the post-Alex Ferguson era. To prevent further drift and decay, it is essential the club gets the next appointment right. It is time to hand the reins to... Antonio Conte.

Conte has been linked with the job before. He was a candidate following Jose Mourinho’s sacking, but United ended up sticking with Ole Gunnar Solskjaer after an impressive spell as interim boss. When Solskjaer himself came under pressure in the autumn of 2021, reports in Italy indicated Conte was interested in replacing him. But the call never came.

United were supposedly deterred by Conte’s combative nature. They feared he was a short-term option rather than a manager who would rebuild the club over several years. If United were to let those same concerns rule Conte out as Carrick's successor, they would be making a grave mistake.

Granted, Conte is unlikely to build a dynasty at Old Trafford. Since leaving Juventus in 2014, he has not completed more than two seasons with any club. And there is no doubt he is combustible. Conte is more kick-up-the-backside than arm-around-the-shoulder and not everyone in the United squad would respond well to his methods.

Still, Conte’s track record speaks for itself. He has won six league titles with four different teams. In his last five club roles, he has only failed to scoop silverware at Tottenham Hotspur. Even there, Conte brought about an initial upturn, guiding Spurs into the Champions League at Arsenal’s expense in 2021/22.

It is not as if he has only ever taken over teams on the verge of success. With United surely to soon be looking for another man to revive a fallen giant, they should note that Conte led Juventus to their first Serie A success post-Calciopoli in 2012. Both Chelsea and Napoli finished 10th the year before Conte’s arrival; he won the league in his debut campaign at both clubs. At Inter, Conte ended an 11-year wait for a scudetto in 2021.

United cannot afford to be too precious about Conte’s tendency to move on quickly. Their recent managerial picks have only lasted one or two years anyway. At least Conte would give the club a better chance of success during his own short stay.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Conte’s reputation for putting noses out of joint would be no bad thing for United, a sleeping giant in need of a rude awakening. The Italian has the force of personality to drag the club out of its malaise. It is certainly hard to imagine players being openly critical of his tactics, as Bruno Fernandes was of Carrick’s after the defeat by Como. Conte would command instant respect in the dressing room.

Of course, there is no guarantee Conte would succeed at Old Trafford. United have tried virtually everything since Ferguson retired, going back to the drawing board more often than an overworked town planner. The club’s problems run much deeper than the manager. Would anyone really be surprised if they were in the exact same position in two or three years’ time?

Failure is not inevitable, though, and despite the understandable doom and gloom, United’s squad does contain talent. Conte would quickly make them more competitive, and morale would rise with improving results. This season is not a write-off yet. But if United want to salvage something from it, there is only one man they need to call.

Derby County vs Norwich City. Sky Bet Championship.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Derby County and Norwich City at Pride Park on Tuesday night; Canaries pile more pressure on struggling Rams and their boss John Eustace.

Norwich piled more pressure on Derby boss John Eustace after thrashing the Championship strugglers 4-0 at Pride Park.

On his 47th birthday, Eustace saw his side ripped apart by the pace and movement of the Canaries, who scored three times before the break.

Anthony Musaba, Paris Maghoma and Darlin Yongwa put Norwich in complete control before substitute Jovon Makama wrapped up a third straight win for the visitors and condemned Derby to a fourth defeat in five games.

Derby have won only once this season and Friday night's home game with Bolton now looks like a huge one for Eustace.

They went into the game as only one of two teams without a home win in the Championship and they fell behind in the eighth minute. Jack Stacey crossed from the right and although Yongwa's header was saved, Musaba slammed the rebound into the roof of the net.

Musaba had a great chance to score his second in the 15th minute when Andre Brooks played him in but his low shot struck the legs of goalkeeper Jacob Widell Zetterstrom.

Norwich looked like scoring every time they came forward and after Zetterstrom made a reflex save to deny Mathias Kvistgaarden, Maghoma made it two with a curling effort from the edge of the box in the 27th minute.

Boos rang out from the home fans and only the woodwork denied Norwich a third when Stacey's shot hit the inside of a post and was cleared off the line by Alex Mowatt.

The half-time whistle was met with another chorus of disapproval from the home fans and it was no surprise when Derby made three substitutions for the second half.

Derby at least had an effort on target with a Carlton Morris header forcing Daniel Grimshaw into a diving save and there was certainly more urgency about their play but Norwich were not finished.

Makama came to the party in the 66th minute with a rasping drive from the edge of the area which Zetterstrom could not keep out.

That was the signal for Derby fans to head for the exits and some of those who stayed joined in when Norwich fans taunted Eustace with chants of "sacked in the morning".

It was certainly a miserable night for Eustace and Derby, who even at this early stage look like a team fighting relegation.

#951. Art for freedom: Maria Kalesnikava in Bonn

The Belarusian musician and civil rights activist Maria Kalesnikava held the keynote speech on the importance of art at the 2026 Beethovenfest in Bonn. She also visited DW.

Maria Kalesnikava knows all too well how authoritarian regimes repress art: The Belarusian flautist and activist spent five years in detention as a political prisoner, three of which were in solitary confinement. Speaking at this year's Beethovenfest, she said: "A person's external freedom can be taken away, sometimes almost entirely. Their freedom of movement, contacts with other people, and access to information can be limited." She pointed out that it is, however, much harder to control what has already become part of one's memory, imagination and inner experience. "And it is precisely in this that I find the explanation for why culture is so important for a free society and why authoritarian systems so often view it with distrust" she concluded during the keynote speech.

A key figure of the Belarusian opposition, the artist and political activist was arrested by the regime of Alexander Lukashenko in the summer of 2020, after the regime had violently suppressed the peaceful revolution for democracy and freedom. Across the country, mass protests and a democratic civil rights movement took place after the controversial presidential election on August 9, 2020.

Kalesnikava recalled how, during her imprisonment, she had carried her world and her experiences, with her all along. This enabled her to remain free, and not to feel like a victim. To Kalesnikava, this is precisely the power of art and also the reason why all dictators — whether Stalin, Hitler or Putin and Lukashenko — hate independent arts and culture, even if it's not overtly political.

During a panel discussion in Bonn, Kalesnikava stressed this point directly:

"The question often arises: what are we defending in Ukraine? Why do we need so much money and new weapons? For me, it is completely clear: the war Russia started is not just against Ukraine. It's a war against European values and European culture. It is a war against our civilization." Kalesnikava realized this immediately when she heard about the Russian war against Ukraine in February 2022, while she was imprisoned.

Kalesnikava was released and has been living in freedom again for ten months now — a miracle that she didn't think was possible and an achievement of international diplomacy. The fact that she emerged and returned to her life full of resilience is thanks in part to Beethoven and Bach, as Kalesnikava, who studied the flute and earned a degree in early and new music in Minsk and Stuttgart, recalled. "I spent a lot of time in complete silence. But this silence was almost never empty, because music constantly played in my head," Kalesnikava said in Bonn. "We musicians know this state very well — sometimes a melody or a musical phrase gets so stuck in your head that it's simply impossible to get rid of it. In normal life, this can even be annoying. In prison, I realized for the first time that this could bring great happiness."

During her visit to Bonn, the Belarusian activist also visited DW and appeared as a guest on the DW Russian language show "DW Novosti." Kalesnikava currently lives in Berlin following an invitation by the German government, where she is also recovering from the horrors she experienced. She sees it as her responsibility to remind the world about what is happening to more than 800 political prisoners in Belarus, as well as the importance and fragility of free artistic expression. On October 2, 2026, she held her keynote speech at the Beethovenfest in Bonn as part of a conference titled "Cultural Events as Political Spaces?," organized with the support of the German Federal Cultural Foundation.

More than 200 representatives from concert institutions and music festivals from across Germany came to the newly renovated Beethovenhalle in Bonn for the final weekend of this year's Beethovenfest. Together, they debated innovative forms and formats for music, as well as issues that stretch far beyond the music industry and urge on to think outside the box.

"Arts and culture are not responsible for taking on specific opinions from political parties, or for making explicitly political statements," Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest and host of the conference, told DW. "What art always creates, however, is spaces for encounter, and places where people can tolerate ambivalence. And that is such an important part of our society, that we're able to handle making collective experiences." To Walter, this is precisely where arts and culture come in, as artists create spaces for independent thought, subjective interpretations, as well as doubts. "Perhaps it's true that there is something like a DNA of freedom in the nature of art," Walter explained in an interview with DW.

The festive closing of the 2026 Beethovenfest took place on 3 October, which is also German Unity Day. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra, under the baton of conductor Anja Bihlmaier, performed Johannes Brahms' "A German Requiem," an iconic piece that evokes reconciliation and trust.

After four weeks of Beethovenfest 2026, the festival recorded the highest number of visitors in a decade. Around 35,000 people came to experience, celebrate and discuss art together at more than 100 concerts and events.

This article was written by Andrey Gorezky, translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal and Tenzin Sekhon.

#950. An unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeur

Only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have truly succeeded in the Old Trafford hot seat with each casting uneasy shadows

Should any football club fit the Great Man theory of history it is Manchester United. In the past 100 years, only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have knocked the club into shape. A pair of 20th-century Scotsmen, born 15 miles apart in Bellshill and Govan respectively, found the key. Otherwise, United has been a managerial dustbin, Michael Carrick the latest likely lobbed on the pile.

Busby and Ferguson built the club around themselves, possessing the charisma to convince others that theirs was the path to follow. Carrick, an insider, a club man, is falling victim to the same isolation as his predecessors in failure. Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez going off-piste in TV interviews to depth charge Carrick were actually following club tradition. With glamour comes decadence, the faded grandeur that has so often chased a United manager out the door.

Beyond Busby and Ferguson, each United manager who also served felt the lash of desperation of a falling giant. Each of their defenestrations has featured an infighting that would not have been out of place in ancient Rome. Favouritism, nepotism, self-interest, entitlement, complacency and sentimentality have been the betrayal of a legend, to use the title of Michael Crick’s and David Smith’s “j’accuse” book from 1989. Living with the legend and influence of those two managers leads the list of difficulties.

United fans know such history too well. “You lousy bastards, you let him down,” Brian Kidd told teammates when the bullet came for Wilf McGuinness, Busby’s immediate successor, in December 1970. Busby himself had done the deed. A December 1972 meeting at Selhurst Park with Tommy Docherty as Crystal Palace beat United 5-0 hastened the end for Frank O’Farrell.

Docherty’s turn came. His sacking in 1977 after an affair with the physio’s wife was announced by the club secretary, Les Olive, from behind the oak door of the chairman Louis Edwards’ Cheshire mansion. Dave Sexton was sacked in 1981 despite winning his last seven matches. Falling attendances at “Cold Trafford” did for “Whispering Dave”. Ron Atkinson turned his November 1986 sacking into a party in the office that also housed the club sunbed. Big Ron’s parting gift was the hangovers that greeted Ferguson’s first day in charge.

Ferguson’s predecessors had been intimidated by the fog of pipe smoke wafting down Old Trafford’s corridors. O’Farrell had needed to ask Busby if the former manager could vacate the manager’s office. “A fantasy world” is how O’Farrell described Busby’s coterie of gossipy former players who teed off with “the old man” at Davyhulme golf course. “There was no reality in the myth,” the Corkman dubbed “O’Failure” said in 1991.

Busby’s indulgence of George Best, careering towards oblivion, created problems O’Farrell found unsolvable. Docherty showed the political wiles to jettison Best in January 1974 but also shelling Bobby Charlton, Denis Law and Paddy Crerand created enemies. Falling in love with Mary Brown, with whom Docherty remained for the rest of his life, was enough for a boardroom moral majority to rid themselves of their turbulent manager.

Ferguson’s successors must deal with his continued presence, the face in the crowd photographers and TV directors seek. His patronage of Malcolm Glazer’s 2005 takeover is a dubious legacy dragging down those who have followed him. Ferguson mostly keeps his own counsel, a well-remunerated club ambassador until Sir Jim Ratcliffe cancelled a £2m annual stipend in 2024. There have been slips. “You should always start with your best players,” Ferguson told the mixed martial arts fighter Khabib Nurmagomedov in 2021 when Ole Gunnar Solskjær had dropped Cristiano Ronaldo, loose talk escaping to social media.

Ferguson’s part in Ronaldo’s disastrous return to Old Trafford evidenced continuing back-channel influence, echoing Busby and Best. Carrick, during his press conference last Friday, mentioned his chats with his former boss. The omission of Fernandes for the Bournemouth game, left to sulk on the bench in club tracksuit, was classic Fergie politics.

A Ferguson facsimile is a fool’s errand. Carrick might have learned the lessons dished out to Solskjær, to whom he was assistant. After refusing to use Ferguson’s parking space and misty-eyed chat of “the boss”, nobody was buying the affable, gentle Norwegian cosplaying as a Glaswegian hard man.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Not that an injection of the alpha male has been much more use. Time has been kinder to the Louis van Gaal and José Mourinho regimes as subsequent failures pile up, but both failed to embrace the expectations of attacking football.

Not that other club traditions were avoided. The subterfuge that brought in Mourinho was as dastardly as any of the post-Busby knifings. “People know him as a larger-than-life character,” the executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward said on Van Gaal’s 2014 appointment. “My wife had to find out when she was in the lift with Woodward’s family,” Van Gaal said of finding, in the haze of celebrating the 2016 FA Cup final victory, that he was being replaced. His former Barcelona assistant had successfully lobbied Woodward. Attempts have been made by the Glazers’ operatives and, since December 2023, Ratcliffe’s Ineos, to corporatise and professionalise but United’s innate excess and anarchy keeps overtaking rationale.

Using the means of a Netflix special, Mourinho has retrofitted his part in the story, he and Ferguson revealing together the fact he turned United down in 2013. The inference is that if Mourinho had arrived then all would have been roses. It is an unconvincing attempt at airbrushing both men’s reputations. Where does that leave David Moyes, the immediate successor painted as afterthought? In July 2013, Ferguson was celebrated as kingmaker, Moyes the rightful heir.

Moyes’s reputation is another enhanced by failures that followed, including Mourinho’s grumpy, fractious tenure. When emerging reluctantly from his Lowry Hotel bolthole, the Portuguese reduced himself to mocking club history with “football heritage” rants. Such a scorched-earth policy was echoed by Ruben Amorim, while Erik ten Hag’s retention by Ineos in summer 2024 was as confusing to Ten Hag as to everyone else.

An unmanageable club? Busby and Ferguson showed it can be done, though the chance of another empire recedes the longer the vanity, plotting and self-interest that personify United continues. And for that, Busby and Ferguson deserve a share of the blame.

#949. Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis

AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal has raised questions about machine-generated texts.

It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.

This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven?

These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring.

The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was long-listed for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn.

So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?

"We will have to learn to live with doubt," said Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

Bajohr has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.

Nina George, a bestselling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.

At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform.

George has addressed the European Parliament and the lower house of the German parliament, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she said, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection.

But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier?

US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.

"I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.

In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery.

Hart sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she said, adding that each book reaches more than 5,000 people.

Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."

It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.

For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it.

But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future.

#948. What tech entrepreneurs can teach scientists about failure

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Mary Ryan discusses what industry can teach academia about failure in science. Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Are universities doing enough to help students learn from their mistakes, and allowing them to see setbacks as a spur to creativity and success?

Materials scientist Mary Ryan, Vice-Provost (Research and Enterprise) at Imperial College London, argues that a good training in science should accommodate learning from setbacks, wrong moves and false starts.

Too often, students judge themselves harshly by one poor exam result or failed experiment, she suggests.

In April 2026 Ryan addressed Failure in Science, a conference held at Imperial in partnership with Nature. In the third episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, she says: “People often point to California’s Bay Area as being this hotbed of innovation.

“You can very easily be a serial startup creator there. When you talk to entrepreneurs, one of the first things they tell you is the three companies that they had that failed. That doesn’t preclude them starting a new one and getting funding for it, whereas I think in the UK and probably in Europe in general, there’s more of a requirement for a track record.

“We have to shift that dynamic if the rest of the world is going to catch up with what’s happening in the US.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03485-2

I’m Dr. Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

And in episode three of Failure in Science, a podcast series about how to do science better, we explore failure and institutions.

Yes, we all have our personal failures, our bad times.

But what if it is actually our institutions that are failing us?

What if a rigid system of education is stifling our imagination?

What if the hunt for grants makes us play safe and narrows our thinking?

Jem Woods, who’s a professor at Imperial College London, opened the Failure in Science conference in April with a quote from Albert Einstein:

The quote is, “As our circle of knowledge expands, so does the circumference of darkness surrounding it. And we have to continue to keep on thinking around and being critically reflective on that uncertainty and the parameters of that uncertainty and how we perceive what we know and what we don’t know.”

And I think that sits at the heart of the failure in science questions.

Yes, I’m Mary Ryan. I’m the Vice Provost for Research and Enterprise at Imperial College London, and I’m the Armourers and Brasiers’ Chair for material science.

So what would I say my big failures are? When you see someone who’s clearly, you know, a successful academic?

You know, I have a research group at Imperial College, so in some ways, I’ve been very successful.

And I think it’s hard, particularly for early career researchers, to see people who have you know, quotes, “made it,” reflecting that they had failures.

So I think actually it’s really important that we talk about things that we weren’t successful at.

Every academic has got a folder on their computer of proposals that were rejected, papers that were rejected for one reason or other.

That doesn’t mean those ideas weren’t worthy or valuable.

Some of them were bad, and we had to be told they were bad.

But how you respond to that rejection? I think failure and rejection are intimately entwined, right?

And that shapes who you are as a scientist, actually, how, that you get them, but how you respond to them.

But there are many times where you do an experiment with a certain focus, and that experiment itself might fail, or you miss something in the background.

Famously, in the 1980s and early 90s, everybody that was working on surface science STM. Many surface science approaches would use highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) as a standard substrate.

To make your surface clean, what we did, we’d use a piece of tape. We cleave the surface because graphite cleaves very nicely, as we know.

For about 10 years, literally thousands of people were throwing away bits of graphene on their Sellotape because we were focused on the surface and not what we’d done to clean the surface.

And of course the discovery of graphene using exactly that technique was awarded the Nobel Prize.

And I think that’s just a really interesting reflection that you can be doing a certain piece of work and that is successful, but sometimes you’ve also thrown away what was important.

I think that’s a metaphor for life, probably. By focusing on one thing, you throw away what’s really important.

So at the conference, Professor Jem Woods quoted Einstein’s discussion around the kind of, the circumference of knowledge and what is known and what is not known.

And it’s really challenging from an educational training perspective to get that balance of supporting students to understand what we know, but also understanding that there’s uncertainty at the boundaries of that knowledge.

It’s challenging because that makes assessment more difficult. And there’s a large degree of assessment built into how we teach and train and educate people.

But it’s difficult because it becomes very uncomfortable for both the educator and the student to deal with a space where we just don’t know.

Now, I actually think it’s a brilliant opportunity for thinking about how we design education to really put some of those challenging questions into the hands and minds of students, because I think it’s when there are “What are the big questions of the universe?”

You know, they’ve inspired people for generations. And we’ve still got them.

There’s a danger that we now treat education and knowledge as complete when it’s not. And that means that you’re probably not lighting some of those sparks that we’ve seen before.

I think it’s also really, really important that in a space where knowledge is also increasingly captured and categorized by AI, that there’s a real understanding of people that we train that we don’t have the sum total of knowledge.

We don’t know everything. There’s still uncertainties. There’s still questions.

So you’ve also got to question (when you interact with frontier technology) about what if the knowledge you are being told, what knowledge it has been trained on, what is the boundary of that knowledge as well?

So all of those things mean we have to, I think, bring it further into the centre, what is unknown, before we build on what we do know.

So science is founded on experimentation and with the risk of failure fundamentally at its core.

I’m really, curious, I guess, about the balance between applied science and curiosity-driven, sometimes called fundamental science.

And yet, I wonder, aren’t we all curious? And isn’t it that we all want to be curious?

Isn’t that what drives experimentation and testing and knowledge and knowledge generation?

We’re constantly thinking about narrowing our boundaries.

How do we set our boundaries? And yet, we should always be thinking about how we expand our boundaries, how we remain curious.

Professor Jem Woods made an interesting point at the conference around expanding knowledge and this kind, a bit of a tension between discovery, applied science, and how we think about experimentation in that space.

One of the things I like to just try to take everything back to is when you’re thinking about science and applied science, what are the questions you are asking?

Are you asking a why question? Are you asking a what question? Are you asking a how question?

Because that sort of shapes what kind of an experiment you would design and think about.

If you were to take a, you know, a big step back and think about you know pushing the boundary of discovery science, which are often why questions.

And you have a hypothesis or an idea about you know what the answer is to the why, you should always design your experiment to disprove that hypothesis, right?

That’s the way that science actually progresses.

So you should be designing experiments in some ways that fail, right?

Because you’re testing to get to disprove a hypothesis.

I feel like we’ve lost a little bit of that because those experiments are hard to do. They’re hard to think about. They’re hard to publish.

And so what are the mechanisms, by the way, we capture those disproving of hypotheses as really parts of contribution to knowledge.

Because they narrow down what are the right answers and what are the right ways forward.

I still think we need to make sure we capture that as a really fundamental part of the scientific method when we’re doing our training of students.

But quite often, if you want to really, but again, push the boundaries of what you’re going to be able to deliver, you have to work out where those boundaries are, right?

So you have to get to the point where something doesn’t work to understand what does work.

And I think all of those are places where you start to see, and I’m slightly using works and doesn’t work as a failure version, which is not quite the same.

But I think it’s important that you get to the point when you’ve pushed it as far as you can, the frontier of discovery or applied science.

I’m Roseanne. So I’ve been at Imperial for around four years now.

So I think the failure in education session was very relevant to me because I’ve lived it.

So what I really thought was quite inquisitive was this tension between systemic and individual failure, and how the system might, kind of, create individual failure, but then individual failure can kind of symbolize this systemic failure too.

But I felt that what was really important was to make known to students that failure always carries loads of weight and symbolism within our day-to-day lives, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that we’ve failed.

So during the final plenary session, Rosanne I think, fed back on the failure in education.

And she talked really interestingly about the difference between systemic and individual failures.

And I feel like the failure in education discussion really symbolized this first step towards acknowledging, number one, that education is kind of underpinned by inequalities.

That means that other people might not have the right science capital or kind of social capital to mean that we all carry the same equal understanding of science, and that means that we need to bridge these gaps.

But also at the same time that we need to fulfill students with confidence to be able to, not fail, but to make mistakes that result in improving and acknowledging that failure isn’t failure as we like to symbolize it, but how it drives you towards creating....

One thing that really resonated with me and what she was talking about was this idea that at an individual level, the impact of failure is not equally felt.

And the likelihood of failure is not equal, depending on your social capital, your background, the disparity that we have in educational inputs, and the disparity that failure or perceived failure has on your educational outputs, and your life chances.

And this is a really big challenge for all of us, I think, to deal with as a society and as an education community, how do we level that playing field on the way in, and make sure that we are enabling the brightest people, wherever they come from, with a background, to be able to have an equal chance of success?

But then also on the other side of that, some people are allowed to fail, and still succeed, right? And we know we all recognize that in life. We all have experiences of that.

One of the things I think this is it really incumbent on educational establishments is to think about building resilience.

Right, building resilience in our students so they don’t feel that a single failure of a single exam is a reflection on the totality of what they bring, on their talent and their knowledge and what they’ve been learning.

That actually, it’s seen as a space for increased learning, a space to reflect and go back and say, “Actually I can do better.”

Of course, we live and our systems, I think it’s where it comes to the systemic part. Our systems are built on a, you know, pass fail first two one.

And I think what we need to reflect a little bit on is how we talk about that.

I mean, I think you know I am I am still a believer that we need to train people to the highest level they can, and we need to say that we are bringing the brightest and the best, and giving them as the best education they can, in order that they can go on and change the world, right?

But how do we say within this pool of people, everybody is valuable, and everybody’s contribution is valuable, and your output is going to go on and make a difference.

I guess thinking about why it’s important that we actually embrace the idea of failure has got many, many different reasons in it within a university and education context.

One is, I think, the perception of what success looks like for an early career researcher.

There is still a lingering, if you start off doing research, the ultimate endpoint view is to be an academic professor.

We know the likelihood of that is probably about 5%.

But also we know they’re not necessarily the most impactful jobs, right?

And so one thing that we’ve been doing at Imperial is establishing a new research institute for early career researchers that helps them see multiple pathways.

So what does it look like to have a job in industry? What does it look like to work in policy? To work in publishing? To work in the public sector?

And then think about what are the steps that might get you to those kind of careers very early on, not as a second choice, but as actually “That’s my north star from day one. This is what I want to do with my research.”

And that’s an important reset on expectations and the expectations that you give yourself and the expectations that we, as an organization, give to early career researchers that are here.

The other area I think is really important is on innovation and entrepreneurship.

Those are inherently areas that are high risk.

They should be high risk, and they should be, you know, we talk about failing fast.

What we also find is that when you’re in an academic culture, students don’t like to fail.

You know, you don’t want to fail an exam, you don’t want to fail a test.

So, what we’ve done with our entrepreneurship for our undergraduate programme, we’ve set that up through an entity we call the Enterprise Lab.

We have programmes that train students to think about entrepreneurship, how to bring an idea and turn it into a device or a company.

We link them to entrepreneurs outside of the university.

All of that is deliberately extracurricular, right? So it’s not counted for credit.

They can come in, they can explore their ideas. They can be stupid ideas. They can be brilliant ideas.

But they’re not in a framework where someone’s going to give them an A or a B or a C. They’re going to say, “Did I make a company? Did I not make a company? Did I decide I want to do that? I didn’t want to do that.”

And so it completely changes the culture of how they. Approach that activity, and that’s really important for it to be almost like a safe space to fail.

Or almost a place where failing is one of the positive outcomes because you’ve done something that was disruptive and it didn’t work, and that’s a good outcome.

And now you take that and you take it back to somewhere else.

So creating that culture of, you know, have an idea, try something, fail fast. No consequences other than you learnt something, right?

It’s a really important part of how we think about entrepreneurship.

What are the systems questions around innovation spinouts and failure?

People often point to the to the Bay Area, the US, as being this hotbed of innovation, and one of the reasons for that is you can very easily be a serial startup creator, and you have a startup then it fails, and a startup then it fails.

And in fact, when you talk to entrepreneurs in the Bay Area, one of the first things they tell you is the three companies that they had that failed.

That doesn’t preclude them starting a new one and getting funding for it, whereas I think in the UK and probably in Europe in general, there’s more of a requirement for a track record.

So people who have had multiple startups, typically they’ve all succeeded, right?

And so it’s this difference between at a systems level, how you perceive that failure as being “Well, this is my only one chance, so I’ve got to make it work,“ versus, “I’m going to try three or four times until that one works."

We have to shift that dynamic if the rest of the world is going to catch up with what’s happening in the US.

That means a few things. It means probably more venture capital, venture capital is able to take more risk, but also again that resilience in our individuals.

That if this one thing doesn’t work, they should try again and try again.

#947. Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay

The England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London

Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.
