#909. Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?

The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.

At less than 3 centimeters (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.

In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.

All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."

That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.

Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.

This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.

The risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules."

That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.

Fortunately many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.

It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.

Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.

Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.

Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.

At more than 3 centimeters, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.

Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.

It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.

At 2 milimeters or smaller, the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 milimeters.

The risk of cancer becomes 9%-10% at about 8 to 10 milimeters. And at larger than 1 centimeter, the risk of cancer is about 15%.

The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.

There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.

According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.

A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."

However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.

Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

#908. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

Ever wondered who makes sure your footy video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to."

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

#907. Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Jonathan Wilson

Sunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last season

Arsenal are three points clear at the top of the Premier League table. But given the team in second are Manchester City, who are likely to be facing at the very least a major points deduction, perhaps more significant is that they are five clear of Brighton in third. The season of domination that many anticipated from the champions appears to be coming to pass.

Liverpool challenged them on Sunday. There was a 20-minute spell before half-time when they swarmed all over Arsenal, and Anfield felt at least like it did in the golden years of Jürgen Klopp, when it buzzed with an energy that could overwhelm visitors. But Arsenal got through that, reset at half-time, and navigated the second half with relative comfort. For the second league game running, they denied Liverpool a shot on target.

If there is a lesson, it is that Liverpool, like Brighton, demonstrated that a very aggressive press can unsettle Arsenal. But then, a very aggressive press can unsettle anybody. In Arsenal’s loss at Brighton, Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas took difficult opportunities; at Anfield Liverpool were denied what should surely have been a penalty when Jurriën Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt – another bad moment for VAR, in that the no-call essentially mandated players to go down and highlight contact. Later, Alexis Mac Allister put a free header over. That was the difference, and this Arsenal team will not give opponents many chances. They are good at closing games out. Ezri Konsa in particular was outstanding on Sunday.

They also have a strong bench. The policy has been to make the squad deeper rather than adding the very highest quality – which is why the links with Vinícius Júnior over the summer were so unexpected. That has frustrated some, but it has been successful. Arsenal on Sunday could bring on Myles Lewis-Skelly, Piero Hincapié, Viktor Gyökeres and Mikel Merino to protect their lead with very little diminution of quality. But it’s not just on a man-to-man level that Liverpool’s options suffer by comparison; their changes upset the balance. They never really had control of the game once Dominik Szoboszlai had come on for Trey Nyoni.

It’s been a recurring feature of this season that Arsenal turn half-time draws into full-time wins – it’s already happened seven times. Winning individual games, though, is only part of it; a deeper squad means there can be more rotation, which should help prevent fatigue as the season goes on, as well as providing additional cover when injuries do occur. That said, their depth was not sufficient to get them past Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup last week, although they will face few games in conditions as challenging as those on the Lancashire coast.

There are still three-quarters of the season to go, and Arsenal were in a similarly commanding position at this stage last season, four points clear of second-placed Bournemouth after nine games. The expectation then was for a procession that didn’t materialise and looked, amid a spring wobble, to have gone awry. Then as now the feeling was not merely that Arsenal were very good, but that none of their rivals looked especially threatening.

But this season they have the memory of winning the title; the insecurity of three successive second-place finishes should be lessened. There is a resilience to them that has already brought a first win at Anfield since 2012 and a victory at Nottingham Forest after successive goalless draws at the City Ground. They’re picking up points at grounds where they’ve stumbled.

Last season, City were more resilient than had been anticipated. It may be a different story this time, and not just because of the potential for a savage points deduction. After seven straight wins they have lost successive league games to Aston Villa and Brighton, but the vulnerabilities that have been exposed had been apparent earlier in the season: a high defensive line that can be exploited. Liverpool are starting to coalesce under Andoni Iraola but they haven’t clicked quite yet and are, anyway, nine points adrift. Chelsea are a point better off but still a work in progress. Brighton have probably been the best other side, but they don’t have the depth to be considered a title challenger.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Sunday made clear what was already widely suspected: Arsenal are the best team in the league by some margin. It’s not just their depth, their cohesion and the wide variety of situations from which they can score goals, it’s that they now have belief and are picking up points at places where they have often failed in the past. And if they do build up a substantial lead by Easter, that could be hugely beneficial to their European challenge, which remains the one unconquered frontier.

#905. From VHS dreams to San Siro glory: Amorim’s Milan surge puts rivals on notice | Nicky Bandini

Inspired by the legendary Milan sides of his youth, the manager gave his side a lift with a tactical victory over Inter

Ruben Amorim had waited a lifetime for his first Milan derby. As a kid growing up in Lisbon, he supported two football teams. There was the local one, Benfica, whose games he attended so early in life that his father has recalled changing nappies in the stands of the old Estádio da Luz. And the other one that captivated him from overseas.

“I remember watching tapes of that Milan team with [Paolo] Maldini, [Franco] Baresi, [Ruud] Gullit, [Frank] Rijkaard, [Dejan] Savicevic,” Amorim told the Portuguese newspaper Expresso in 2017. “My childhood dreams were to play for Benfica and Milan. I’ve fulfilled one. Now I suppose I’ll have to become a coach for the other!”

It took him another nine years to achieve that ambition. The Milan side he inherited in June did not look like the continental conquerors he used to admire on VHS. This version had just missed out on the Champions League for a second season running. Its hoped‑for star of this decade, Rafael Leão, was ready to move on amid laments of unfulfilled potential.

Still, from day one, Amorim has given off the air of a cat who got the cream. It was tempting to infer some relief at moving on from an unhappy chapter at Manchester United. Certainly it can’t have hurt that Milan’s owners backed their new manager to a tune of more than €160m (£132m) on transfer fees in the summer window.

But there was something in there too, of a person fulfilling a promise they made to their younger self. “Everybody knows Milan is one of my clubs since I was a boy,” Amorim said. “In my time as a young boy, Milan was the strongest team in Italy. And calcio was the best league in the world.”

Serie A lost that title some time ago. No Italian team have won the Champions League since 2010, and no player representing one has been awarded the Ballon d’Or since 2007. The Premier League long ago surpassed all rival competitions for TV revenues and spending power. Only a handful of super clubs elsewhere have kept up.

And yet, Serie A is having some kind of moment. Its reputation as the home of dour catenaccio is as outdated as Amorim’s old VCR, but things have spun especially far in the opposite direction this season, with an average of 3.18 goals per game. Italy’s top division has become home to some of the giddiest attacking football on the continent. Through almost 10 completed rounds there have been two 0-0 draws.

Bologna 2-1 Monza, Udinese 2-5 Roma, Milan 3-1 Inter, Como 1-0 Venezia, Frosinone 2-0 Torino, Lazio 2-1 Cagliari, Lecce 1-2 Genoa, Juventus 2-0 Napoli

Monday: Sassuolo v Fiorentina (5.30pm GMT), Atalanta v Parma (7.45pm GMT)

Amorim’s Milan have played their part. On Wednesday they endured their first league defeat, a barmy 4-2 loss at home against Bologna in which they fell behind early, came back to lead before half‑time then collapsed after the interval. Their manager cited exhaustion. An ominous thought, leading into the derby on Saturday. Inter had dropped only two points all season. Even their one draw felt more like a win, coming from two goals down to get a result away at Roma. Reigning champions, who reinforced the deepest squad in Serie A with the English trio of Curtis Jones, John Stones and Djed Spence in the summer, the Nerazzurri have been strong favourites to retain their title.

But after waiting a lifetime for a part in this fixture, Amorim was never going to arrive unprepared. If anything, the defeat by Bologna might have been influenced by his keeping one eye on the derby. Luka Modric and Christian Pulisic were left out of the starting XI in midweek, coming on only as second-half substitutes. Both lined up at kick-off against Inter. So did several other starters who had been deemed unfit even for a place on the bench against Bologna – Mario Gila, Adrien Rabiot and Diego Moreira. Amorim sprung a surprise on top of that by naming the 20-year-old Sankhoun Diawara, whose only previous Milan start had been at centre-back, as his left wing-back in a 3-4-2-1.

The manager has shown more tactical flexibility at Milan than he did in Manchester, alternating his back three with a four. In the biggest game of his Milan tenure to date, however, Amorim returned to what he knows best. And Cristian Chivu copied him.

Inter’s manager was grappling with an availability crisis up front. Lautaro Martínez has been out for weeks with a hamstring strain, while Francesco Pio Esposito and Ange-Yoan Bonny were unfit to start due to a virus. Chivu adapted by pushing Andy Diouf, a former midfielder who has been thriving at wing-back, forward to play on the right shoulder of Marcus Thuram, with Petar Sucic on the left.

But where the Nerazzurri looked unsure of themselves in a new system, Milan were straight into their stride. Pulisic put them in front in the fourth minute, his thumping header from Moreira’s cross the culmination of 80 seconds of unbroken possession. Rabiot then made it 2-0 in the 10th minute with a magnificent first-time flick across his body at a corner.

Inter’s defending, on both occasions, was horrendous, but that can be acknowledged without diminishing Milan’s design. The Rabiot goal was a rehearsed training ground routine, Diawara crossing paths with the Frenchman and blocking Hakan Calhanoglu’s attempts to track. Moreira was also flawless in his deliveries. The derby became his breakout moment, showing why Milan spent more than €50m to sign him from Strasbourg this summer.

Inter have recovered from losing positions five times already in this Serie A season, and three times from 2-0 down. They were threatening to repeat the trick after Alessandro Bastoni pulled a goal back from a corner. Spence forced a sensational save from Mike Maignan. But Milan won a free-kick, 20 yards out on the right. Moreira asked Modric to let him take it, then whipped a left‑footed shot over the wall into the near side of the net.

The game finished 3-1 to Milan, Inter’s first league defeat and a huge lift for Amorim. Despite being unbeaten themselves before the midweek defeat by Bologna, the Rossoneri have not always convinced. Even when controlling the tempo of games, they seem to lack clarity in the final third. Gonçalo Ramos, the club’s record signing, has not looked a natural fit as a lone striker, dropping deep too often when his team need a presence inside the box. He has scored just twice in 10 starts since his €73m move from Paris Saint-Germain.

Even this win raised questions. Can it really be the long-term vision for Moreira, the right wing‑back, to frequently hold a position on the pitch higher than the centre-forward?

Amorim was quick to insist on Saturday that no one should get carried away. He expressed delight for supporters and described the experience of his first Milan derby as unlike any other game of which he had been a part. But he also said Milan had been only good, not great, and noted that the three points here were only the same number they would have got by beating Bologna.

A sensible line to take. Milan have dominated this fixture lately – winning the past four derbies across all competitions and staying unbeaten in the past eight. Yet they have not finished above their neighbours since 2021-22, their last Scudetto-winning campaign.

Still, beating your greatest rival is always better than the alternative. The club’s owner, Gerry Cardinale, has been vocal in backing the new manager, telling La Gazzetta dello Sport last week that he was all in on “Amorim ball”. But in the week that Milan and Inter jointly presented plans for the new stadium that will replace San Siro in 2031, this result added weight to his assertion that the Rossoneri can contend for a Scudetto too.

#904. Why are some football shin pads so small?

Liverpool striker Lewis Koumas (second from left) sported low socks and small shinpads on his full Premier League debut at Anfield

Liverpool's Lewis Koumas made his full Premier League debut against Manchester City on Sunday.

While doing so, he sported some very low socks over what appeared to be a very small shin pad.

Last season, images of Burnley's Marcus Edwards went viral after the 27-year-old was seen wearing barely visible shin pads during a Premier League match against West Ham.

Two years ago, a picture of teenager Harry Howell celebrating with James Milner while they were Brighton team-mates also gained attention after fans noticed the visible difference in the size of their shin pads.

Howell's 'micro' pair were an obvious contrast to Milner's far more traditional-sized guards.

So what is behind the trend of extra-small shin guards, and why are they used instead of regular-sized pairs?

The simple answer is that players can choose what size shin pads they want to wear.

The International Football Association Board (Ifab), responsible for the laws of the game, say that shin pads are a mandatory piece of equipment players must wear while playing.

Be of an appropriate size to provide reasonable protection and be covered by the socks

And players are responsible for the size and suitability of their shin pads

The law does not define what an "appropriate" shin pad size is, but leave that decision to each individual player.

Shin pads provide vital protection for players to prevent serious injuries.

There has been a rising trend in younger footballers, as well as some big stars, wearing small shin pads during matches.

The reason for this could be for more comfort and to allow players to move around with greater ease.

Referees are only required to check that some form of shin guards are being worn, Ifab told BBC Sport.

Ifab said players - or the parents or guardians of youth players - must take responsibility for their own safety on the pitch.

While shin pad size is ultimately an individuals choice, any decisions around player safety would also be made in consultation with their club and medical staff.

Marcus Edwards last year was seen wearing very small shin pads for Burnley in the Premier League

Grassroots football teams have started to ban small shin pads for safety reasons.

There are concerns that small shin pads do not cover the shins properly, which can lead to an increased risk of injury - especially at non-elite level.

In August 2024, a football club banned small shin pads after a youth player suffered a double leg break.

Penistone Church player Alfie Collins broke his tibia and fibula in a tackle during a game. The teenager's shin pads, which were no bigger than a credit card, were similar to a size recently worn by some stars of the professional game.

Shin pads "play an important role in injury prevention as they are intended to protect the shin from injury", the Football Association said.

"'Micro' or 'mini' shin pads may therefore increase the risk of injury due to the smaller amount of shin covered compared to larger sized shin pads," they added.

#903. Led by Liam Rosenior and backed by billionaires, Paris FC are now a force in Ligue 1 | Luke Entwistle

After a huge summer and with PSG’s other rivals falling away, their city rivals are aiming to ‘be one of the biggest clubs in Europe’

It is hard to know what Pierre Ferracci found stranger: the fact that he was fully suited among a set of bare-chested Paris FC ultras singing his name or that, behind him, in what was the final game of his presidency, his team were playing Monaco off the park. “I didn’t see any of the first 15 minutes of the game because I was with the ultras,” he admitted. On the pitch, as well as in the stands, was evidence of how far his side has come since he joined back in 2006.

At that time, Les Parisiens were in the amateur third tier of French football. Ferracci arrived initially in an administrative function before becoming owner and president in 2012. It was not until 2017 that his side reached Ligue 2.

It is Ferracci’s work that made the club ripe for investment in what had been seen as a one-club capital, an anomaly in Europe. But it is thanks to his successor and the new owners, the Arnault family, that the club now harbour very serious European ambitions.

Ferracci remained as president and with a significant share when the Arnaults, the owners of the luxury goods brand LVMH and seventh on the Forbes rich list in 2026, bought a majority share in 2024. It was intended that Ferracci would remain as president until the end of the season, at which point he would part ways with his remaining share. His share remains for now, but his role in the running of the club is now over.

“You have to know when to stand aside,” he said on Sunday. The timing feels right. The years of toiling in the lower divisions and the multiple near misses at promotion are in the past; they belong to the Ferracci era, which felt part of the past even when it was still the present. While he will remain as honorary president, he will take a backseat role as the club look to hit new heights.

Liam Rosenior has been appointed to take them there. Fresh from his failed stint at Chelsea, the Englishman had intended to take time out of the game but was tempted by the project, more similar to the one that he took at Strasbourg than the one that he inherited mid-season in the Premier League.

Rosenior’s management style has a greater effect on aspiring players, and at Paris FC there are plenty of those. Rudy Matondo, Patrick Zabi, Luca Koleosho and Pablo Pagis, signed over the summer, all have bright futures. Few clubs in French football could afford such stars.

It is Paris’s new signings that did the business against Monaco. Pagis excelled, running rings around Lamine Camara and Denis Zakaria in midfield, but it was Lassine Sinayoko who was once again the star of the show, contributing to all goals in a 3-1 win.

The Malian scored two and set up Pagis for the third. He has now had a hand, either scoring or assisting, in 13 of Paris’s 16 goals this season. After his impressive form at Auxerre last season, it was a surprise that others didn’t take a gamble on the 26-year-old forward. Their loss is Paris’s gain.

It was Sinayoko’s hat-trick that gave Paris a 3-2 win against Marseille. His brace and last‑minute penalty secured a dramatic 4-3 win against Rennes. Further wins against Strasbourg and Nice and a draw against Lyon have Les Parisiens where they wanted to be, albeit ahead of schedule.

Paris FC Féminines are already a powerhouse on the European scene and the men’s team want to emulate their success. “The long-term target is to be one of the biggest clubs in the country. We want to be one of the biggest clubs in Europe, and I know that is one of the aims of the ownership,” Rosenior said this week.

Outplaying Filipe Luís’s Monaco suggests Paris are on the right track. Their rivals are toiling: Monaco have dropped off, Rennes lack consistency, Lyon are about to lose their manager, Paulo Fonseca, Marseille’s prospects are limited by financial constraints and clubs such as Lens and Lille are unpredictable, given the inexperience in their respective dugouts.

It would, however, be unfair to characterise this Paris side as a challenger by default. And the pace of change is remarkable. It was only this year that the club recruited Antoine Kombouaré, a managerial firefighter, to spare them an immediate return to Ligue 2.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

What a difference one summer can make. Paris spent almost €80m in the window, the third‑highest total in Ligue 1; no side in France’s top-flight had a higher net spend (-€72m) by the end of the summer. Therein lies the impact of wealth in a league that is lacking it.

That the effect is felt so acutely and so immediately on the pitch, however, is also a reflection of a strategy and a vision that, with Rosenior and a focus on youth, is perfectly coherent. Paris Saint‑Germain, whose hegemony Paris FC seek to challenge, floundered for years following the arrival of their new owners but Paris FC know where they want to go, how they want to get there, and are well on their way.

Le Havre 1-5 PSG, Nice 5-2 Rennes, Lille 1-0 Lens, Troyes 2-0 Le Mans, Strasbourg 5-1 Auxerre, Lyon 2-0 Angers, Paris FC 3-1 Monaco, Marseille 2-0 Toulouse

Didier Digard became the first Ligue 1 manager to lose his job this season following Le Havre’s 5-1 loss to PSG, which left the Normandy club with just two points from their opening nine games. Le Havre’s president, Jean-Michel Roussier, was opposed to the decision to relieve Digard, the second longest-serving manager in the league prior to his dismissal, of his duties. He has therefore resigned, while reports in France state that sporting director Demba Ba has also left his role, which the former Newcastle striker only took up over the summer. A whole club rebuild mid-season? The club’s Blue Crow owners have an unenviable task. It was Achraf Hakimi who did the damage for PSG and consigned Digard to the sack. The Moroccan has been popping up in goalscoring positions all season, and he was involved in all five goals, scoring a hat-trick and setting up Mika Godts and Senny Mayulu for the other two. Five wins in a row in the league have shot PSG to the top of the table and allayed the concerns that their start-of-season form had generated.

Not your usual Derby du Nord as Lille hosted Lens on Friday night. Lens had banned their own fans from the away end, a punishment for their dangerous pyrotechnic antics away to Club Brugge in the Champions League That had already incited Uefa to ban the French club’s fans from their next two European away games. It was also a derby lacking the usual pre-match noise, with Davide Ancelotti and Yannick Cahuzac turning down the volume in a game dubbed the “duel of the novices”. But this was perhaps a coming-of-age moment for Ancelotti. At the very least, it was LOSC’s best performance under the Italian manager, son of Carlo. Olivier Giroud’s late goal rewarded a dominant performance from Lille. With Benjamin André and Nabil Bentaleb also starring, it was the experienced heads who did the business for their inexperienced coach.

#902. 125 years of Thomas Mann's 'Buddenbrooks'

This over 1,000-page masterpiece offers a panoramic view of society in the 19th century and exposes the collapse of a merchant family: unrecognized sons, disillusioned daughters and the loss of middle-class ideals.

Who would have imagined it in the beginning? A 26-year-old man without a high school diploma, but greatly ambitious, writes a two-pound book with a melancholy undertone. "I'm not exactly delighted," his publisher initially responded. But he ended up publishing the novel anyway, more out of goodwill than conviction. And the rest is history.

For many, Thomas Mann's Buddenbrooks is considered THE German social novel. It is indeed a classic, and one that garnered the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. Global fame, an international best-seller, and required reading for many German students. Anyone who mentions Thomas Mann thinks of Buddenbrooks in the same breath. Why is that?

Does the explanation lie in the autobiographical connections between the work and the author?

Thomas Mann was born in Lübeck to a merchant family, but his artistic aspirations did not fit in well in the middle-class mainstream. This struggle inspired Mann's first work. The inability of this sensitive bohemian to carry on the family's time-honored business after the death of his father was sniffed at and derided.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reflecting the situation of his novel's character Hanno, Mann had a privileged life in a wealthy family, but one that was at risk of collapse. The aspiring novelist also had to withstand disappointing the expectations of others. He was forced to defend his dream of an artistic life. Yet as much as he was inspired by real life, he forcefully altered these biographical details to place his unique literary mark on his writing.

But does that really matter in light of people who choose not to make the distinction between an author's life and his work? Even though the name "Lübeck" does not appear in the novel, citizens there felt markedly insulted after the publication of Buddenbrooks in 1901.

That likely lies in the fact that the image the author portrayed was not one of an idyllic northern German city, but one of a place that had difficulty blending tradition with modernity.

This contradiction is also seen in each of the figures in the novel. Nothing is like it appears. Mann lays down this foundation of this skepticism from the very beginning, in a scene taking place on a very ordinary Thursday in October 1835. The Buddenbrook family comes together for their ordinary late lunch.

"There they all sat, on heavy, high-backed chairs, consuming good heavy food from good silver plates, drinking full-bodied wines and expressing their views freely on all subjects. When they began to talk shop, they slipped unconsciously more and more into dialect, and used the clumsy but comfortable idioms that seemed to embody to them the business efficiency and the easy well-being of their community. Sometimes they even used an over-drawn pronunciation by way of making fun of themselves and each other, and relished their clipped phrases and exaggerated vowels with the same heartiness they did their food."

There sits the leader of the family company, Johann Buddenbrook the Elder, and his wife, his son and counsel Jean, along with his family. The grandchildren are also there: Tony the dreamer, the quarrelsome rebel Christian, and Thomas, the eldest grandchild.

It is Thomas who is supposed to later take on the responsibility of continuing the family tradition, regardless of the cost. Mann weaves his narrative work starting with this main family, and then across several generations.

But appearances in the family are deceptive. The reader senses it's all headed toward a downfall. The new house is taken over from a family that was once as illustrious as the Buddenbrooks, but faced financial ruin and had to leave.

Johann and his family aim to make a better go of it. They make decisions on what is demanded economically, but fail — financially, interpersonally, and mentally.

Tony and Thomas end up falling in love with people not befitting their social standing, but do not have the courage to stand up to their parents. They enter marriages of convenience, yet it is these partnerships that paradoxically set disaster in motion.

From an early age, Thomas Mann was influenced by Schopenhauer's pessimistic notion of the will being a blind force at work in the world. Thus, there is likewise no escape for the Buddenbrooks. They speak of emotions and morality, yet it is money and economics that steer the ship. Failure, decline and even death seem to be the only viable outcome.

Mann also punctuates this hopelessness in a stylistic manner, by consistently repeating entire passages word for word, or evoking motifs such as the family registry or the estate in all their various forms.

The extent of this demise appears linguistically molded and exaggerated. The Buddenbrooks, this proud north German family of refinement, actually speaks the vernacular studded with empty French expressions. "Je, den Düwel ook, c'est la question, ma très chère demoiselle!"

The lowly servants, the courtesans, and the demi-monde: all of them speak the language of the street, raw and unpolished. In a virtuoso manner, Thomas Mann orchestrated this mass of voices into a panorama of society in the 19th century. The snobbishness on the part of the Buddenbrooks thus appears as a relic of a long lost time. It's a symbol of their inability to adapt to change and place their faith in progress.

Yet the fact that this extensive work spanning several generations does not get weighed down by aesthetic excess is purely due to Mann's brilliance as an author. He is able to bring every one of his numerous characters to life in words. Life that is full of complexity, contradictions and ambiguities. Some of these characters accompany the reader page for page; others appear only briefly.

And yet one begins to contemplate how someone like Grünlich could become a dodgy, unscrupulous husband and catches oneself wanting to chase the fearful Hanno out of the music conservatory and yell to him: "Go, throw yourself into life! You are not a failure." It is precisely this empathy that spurs one on to read through the night and prompts one to chuckle at all the intricate sentences and philosophical digressions.

Thomas Mann: Buddenbrooks, Vintage Classics / Penguin Random House, (German title: Buddenbrooks, 1901). English translation: John E. Woods

Thomas Mann was born into a privileged Lübeck merchant family in 1875. He died in Zurich, Switzerland in 1955. "I am a townsman, a citizen, a child and a great-grandchild of German bourgeois society," the author once wrote about himself. Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 for his debut novel, Buddenbrooks. He also garnered numerous other prizes and honors for his extensive work, including Death in Venice (1911), The Magic Mountain (1924), and the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers (1933-1943). He emigrated to Switzerland in 1933, and to the US in 1938. From there, he made his famous radio commentaries in which he agitated against the Nazis. He returned to Switzerland in 1952.

This article was first published as part of the series 100 German must-reads.

#901. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#900. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk midfielder Marlon Gomes is on three yellow cards, putting him on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

#899. Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family

Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture

Ever since the Observer Sport Monthly published a list of 50 sporting things you must do before you die with Watch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Aires at No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire.

Things have changed, though, and Sunday at La Bombonera (Boca’s stadium known as the Chocolate Box) was quite a different spectacle. Since 2013 football matches in Argentina have been played without visiting fans, so for starters the colour palette has been greatly reduced. The absence of the opposing tribe has been welcomed by many, making the experience of going to a football match more family-friendly and increasing ticket availability for club members.

As we shared a choripán in a corner grill before the game, the Argentinian journalist Ezequiel Fernández Moores recalls the first Superclásico without away fans, at the Monumental in 2013. As Boca’s Emmanuel Gigliotti scored to give the away team the lead, in the press area Moores heard the beginning “G” of someone ready to shout the goal with glee, suddenly realising “non-home joy had to be repressed”.

Over the years the absence of away fans has been mirrored in an absence of away press. Now the journalists sit at their desks along the same height as the middle tier of the traditional home end, where the heart of the hardcore organised gang known as La Doce leads the rhythm section, creating a sense of continuum, with hacks clad in Boca strips cursing and cheering along with the crowd.

Rain had been forecast for Sunday so Boca distributed blue and yellow umbrellas which opened in sync and matched the colour of the smoke from the fireworks organised by the club.

The pyrotechnics used to be smuggled in by La Doce, who would also orchestrate the release of blue and golden balloons at the exact time the players emerged from the tunnel. When I went to pick up my accreditation, the head press officer announced to no one in particular that this “Señora” (meaning me) had once interviewed José Barritta. A young man holding a newborn baby and a couple of kids who looked barely out of school just stared. “The day of the Ambush,” I stated by way of explanation.

Barritta was the infamous leader of La Doce decades ago and in 1994 I did indeed spend the afternoon with him to write a colour piece about the Superclásico from the “middle tray” (the terraces are tiered in three balconies and the middle one is the centre of operations). It was an afternoon that would end in tragedy with two River Plate fans shot dead after the game. Disgustingly, graffiti emerged nearby soon afterwards reading “River 2 Boca 2”, equating two young lives to the two goals River had scored against Boca securing their victory.

My feature was shelved and instead I became a witness to the fact that Barritta had not been involved, my work published in a human rights journal, and my interest in football-related violence swiftly losing the wide-eyed fascination.

Death at the Superclásico was not something new, even then. In 1968, 71 fans – mostly Boca – were crushed when one of the exit gates for away supporters didn’t fully open. Known as the incident of Puerta 12, much of what actually happened remains unknown, but El Gráfico reported the following year’s game saw members of both Boca and River fans chant together against the police. In those days both gangs were friendly, with then-Boca gang leader Quique, who ran a grill opposite the stadium, buying meat from River gang leader “El Tano Mingo”, who was a butcher. They would often join forces and combat against other club gangs well into the mid-1970s when the leaderships changed. Barritta took the helm of La Doce in 1981, by which time the rupture was total.

In 2018 Boca and River met in the Libertadores final, South America’s version of the Champions League, and the Argentina president, Mauricio Macri, thought it might be fun to show the world what a colourful spectacle the Superclásico might be, so away fans were allowed back to the stadium in a one-off experiment. After the Boca bus was attacked with stones and crowd control fell apart around the inner ring surrounding the River stadium, fans were kept under strict orders to remain in place for close to five hours while the powers that be discussed options. The match was cancelled and outrageously moved to Madrid, where one could argue the soul of the Superclásico has remained, if it hadn’t been sucked out already.

Sunday’s game was not a fixture of the calibre of a Libertadores final. In fact, the strangeness of the current system in Argentina means it was almost inconsequential for either cup or league, although a total points system known as the Argentina Table has implied that Boca’s underwhelming 1-0 victory against a River side down to nine men by the end means Boca have a place in next year’s Libertadores.

“I’ve seen better Superclásicos,” said the radio commentator Victor Hugo Morales in his tiny cabin at the stadium. He was commemorating 60 years to the day of his very first radio commentary, back in Uruguay in 1966. I went along to exchange greetings, as I was commemorating 60 years to the day of being alive. “But I’ve also seen worse,” he added.

That must be debatable, though I’ve probably not seen as many as him. The derby doesn’t always offer the best football, often too embroiled in the hype and the media frenzy surrounding it, and the massive banners and flags obscuring the view for most of the pitch. I started going to the Bombonera with my cousins as a teenager, and the most poignant memory of the fixture was taking my 10-year-old brother along without telling my dad. In those days, women and children got in for free. On Sunday, tickets were going for half a million pesos (£240).

I remember grabbing the little boy by the waist of his trousers as I saw him flying above a sea of sweaty men, as I heard someone shout: “Careful you lot, there’s a ‘Señora’ here!” I was 20. I felt perfectly safe, but I couldn’t convey that to my furious father, who I don’t think I’d ever seen so angry, before or since.

Years later, when TV rights took possession of the industry and football became pay-per-view, my dad was one of the early adopters of a codified system which enabled live watching. I suggested our dear family friend Klaus, a River fan, desperate to watch the Superclásico, join my brothers and cousins atDad’s. Klaus didn’t reveal his allegiance and sat quietly in grief while the assorted Boca fiends jumped about in joy when they won. The anecdote is remembered fondly to this day in my family but for him it was a particularly unpleasant experience.

Maybe new generations will be better at bridging the cultural crack. Streamer Davo, the face of new sports media, was nonchalant before the game. “Don’t give me all this Superclásico nonsense. For me, nothing changes if River beats us this game. I’m focused on the Argentina Cup, on the South American final … this is just another match.”

Also seemingly oblivious to the hyped-up frenzied vitriol, my own son had suggested we go to the game together. He, a River fan, however, could not in any realistic sense attend. I’d love to go to a Superclásico with my son, neither one of us banned by the other’s tribe. Maybe one day.

#898. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#897. Asian Cup postponement leaves Socceroos, FA and coach Tony Popovic at crossroads | Joey Lynch

The most immediate question thrown up by the delay of the tournament in Saudi Arabia is what it now means for Popovic

Confirmation that the Asian Cup has been postponed until December 2027 would have caught few by surprise. But the timing of Tuesday’s announcement might have, given it came well ahead of the late November timeframe hinted at by the AFC. Yet with Houthi attacks continuing across Saudi Arabia, it felt inevitable the tournament would be deferred.

However foreseeable though, it has left the Socceroos, their coach Tony Popovic and Football Australia at a crossroads.

It is a major tournament the Socceroos harboured hopes of winning. Japan would have been considered favourites; the Samurai Blue, despite having been underachievers since winning in 2011, have earned that mantle. But, despite back-to-back quarter-final exits, Australia are also acknowledged as a continental heavyweight by their peers, coming off a World Cup in which they were one of only two Asian sides to progress to the knockout stages. And with rivals such as Qatar, South Korea and Iran all aging and/or experiencing significant upheaval, the regional picture suggested they should have challenged in January.

Popovic would have been able to take to Saudi Arabia a side brimming with young talent and boasting an enviable combination of consistent improvement and valuable World Cup experience. They would have been building on an October window in which they twice met Brazil and a pair of ideal preparatory games against the 2023 Asian Cup finalists, Qatar and Jordan, in November.

Even with fitness concerns hovering over Mohamed Touré and Jordy Bos, the talent and momentum was there for the Socceroos to win a second Asian crown.

Nonetheless, there are silver linings. The tournament may benefit from a 12-month delay, as it will feel less like a post-World Cup afterthought. The postponement could also allow the Socceroos to further evolve and become even better by Christmas next year.

Another 11 months means further development, both for the Socceroos as a collective and for individuals such as Nestory Irankunda, Paul Okon-Engstler, Alessandro Circati and Lucas Herrington. Following their recent high-profile moves to some of Europe’s biggest clubs and leagues, that progression could be significant. It also allows for injured players such as Bos, Touré and Lewis Miller time to recover, while other youngsters yet to establish themselves get more time to impress.

In this scenario, the hope is that a bird in the hand isn’t worth two in the bush – that more injuries don’t strike and that veterans such as Jackson Irvine and Aziz Behich maintain their current form.

But the more immediate question arising from the announcement is what it means for Popovic. The November window is now ostensibly the 53-year-old’s last as Socceroos coach; the contract extension he signed ahead of the World Cup, which was supposed to take him through this tournament, concludes on a definitive date rather than a nebulous “post Asian Cup” marker.

Popovic and Football Australia face a challenge neither would have expected when they hammered out – at the coach’s insistence – a deal that only took him through to the end of the continental showpiece. A similar scenario confronts Graham Arnold with Iraq, while Japan have already signalled that Hajime Moriyasu will be replaced by Go Oiwa.

Sign up for expert analysis from Jonathan Wilson as well as a rundown of Australians playing in the major leagues

Is it now simply a matter of extending Popovic’s deal through to 21 January 2028? Given the federation offered him that longer-term deal, and executives such as Heather Garriock and Martin Kugeler have never been anything but effusive in their praise, it’s almost certain Popovic would be able to if he wants. But does he?

He would have had his reasons for not wanting to be locked into a longer-term deal. And as a football-obsessed workhorse, it’s entirely possible he’d have ambitions to return to the grind of club football. His stock is high after leading the Socceroos to the World Cup’s knockout stages, and further bolstered by a window where his side performed well against Brazil and he drew praise from Carlo Ancelotti. If he wants a new challenge, he has earned one.

But what if he stays, only to depart after another 12 months? Kevin Muscat has always appeared to be an obvious successor, especially given he’ll be a free agent after the imminent conclusion of the Chinese Super League. And if Popovic does opt to depart, he should be offered the job. But would he – or another preferred candidate – be willing to wait a year, especially with World Cup qualification will still beginning in September? Does Football Australia risk being left to scramble come 2028 if they don’t play their cards right?

Just like seemingly everything else in Australian football, the postponement of the Asian Cup presents as both a potential opportunity and a curse.

#896. Cunha completes wild Man Utd comeback win over Roma from two down

Manchester United vs Roma. UEFA Champions League.

Match report as Manchester United beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League despite being two goals down at half-time. Bruno Fernandes scored a penalty and Matheus Cunha scored two to complete the comeback before being sent off late on

Football Features Writer @ghostgoal

Manchester United produced an extraordinary comeback from two down to beat Roma 3-2 at Old Trafford and pick up their first win in 10 games.

Michael Carrick looked on the brink when his disjointed team were completely undone for Matias Soule's opener and Donyell Malen soon made it two from the penalty spot. But Matheus Cunha won one of his own, scored two and was sent off in a wild contest.

United had been booed off at the break and when Carlos Baleba had to go off early in the second half with a hamstring injury it all looked dismal for United. But when Cunha won a penalty that Bruno Fernandes scored after a retake it altered the momentum.

Bryan Mbeumo struck both posts with one shot soon after and the noise inside Old Trafford was astonishing thereafter. Roma cleared one off the line and United had two more penalty shouts as the Italian side - unbeaten in Serie A - began to wobble badly.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leonardo Balerdi's error proved it, his woeful clearance allowing Cunha to slot home the leveller. And it was the same player with a stunning near-post finish from Shea Lacey's pass who completed the comeback to the delight of the disbelieving crowd.

Cunha was sent off for a silly foul to ensure a tense finale but United held on for a first win in 54 days. Improbably, Carrick left the pitch not just to applause but having presided over a win in the Champions League. And a spirited one at that.

Where on earth did that come from? Roma were two up and it could have been more against a United side whose spirit appeared as broken as their tactics in a first half that seemed like surrender. But strange things can still happen at the Theatre of Dreams.

It is difficult to overstate the incoherence of those opening minutes. Watching Fernandes throw his arms in the air in disgust at a Baleba pass late in the first half, it looked like a team in disarray and desperate to blame someone else for the situation.

United's tactical setup early on against Roma was arguably even worse than against Como when Fernandes criticised his manager. They were continually cut apart in the left-back position with Diogo Dalot up the pitch and Ayden Heaven exposed.

At that stage, thought turned to the balance of the squad and the quality of it, the confidence and the team spirit, the players, the coach and the ownership. None of that completely goes away after a chaotic 45 minutes but this was at least something.

It was a team telling the fans that they can show spirit, that they are not prepared to let it slide further without a fight, that they can still conjure quality from nowhere. The scenes at the end of the game showed that at this great club, sometimes, that can be enough.

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes speaking to Amazon Prime:

"Fans want to win games, they've been used to seeing this club at the top, winning trophies, winning games every week. For them it's been so frustrating to see the club in this situation.

"I just want to make everyone aware that we're all frustrated with the situation at the moment and we all want to get out of this. Hopefully this win today gives the start of something good for us.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It has been tough, there's been a lot of speculation in the media, a lot of lies around many things that have happened in this club. Between me and the manager, that we had cleared the air, then after, nothing of that happened.

"The manager took a decision of putting myself on the bench [against Bournemouth] because I wasn't performing at that level. Everyone felt that that was a punishment for the words that I had. If it was, it was right.

"The manager is the one that makes the decisions. I have to accept them, I have to go forward with that. It doesn't change the belief I have in the manager, in the staff and every player that is in this club.

"It doesn't change my aim to win every game that I have ahead of me. It should be [a turning point]."

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick speaking in the press conference:

"Proud of a lot of people actually, proud of the players, and they deserve a lot of credit for pulling through that in a tough situation.

"And for the supporters, you know, to be there, they were desperate for us to give them something they could get their teeth into.

"I think it is really important for the players to know what this place can do.

"I am not getting too carried away with things, but it is an important night."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

On the impact of Shea Lacey with his assist for the winning goal:

"Again, not going too over the top, but at the same time, absolutely delighted for Shea. We love him to bits. He is a great young man.

"He is desperate to do well, he has got great ability, so in terms of coming inside and finding a pass, that is not surprising actually, he has got that little glint in his eyes, he plays with a bit of mischief if you like.

"So it is always lovely to have that, but I was just as happy seeing him defending as a right-back when we needed that. I was just as pleased to see him do that on the defensive side.

"I think he gave everybody a bit of a lift coming on the pitch and it was fantastic to see."

#895. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Matty Cash and Matt Crooks are the first players of the 2025-26 Premier League season to pick up a yellow card suspension

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash have become the first players to receive a one-match ban for accumulating five yellow cards in the 2025-26 Premier League season.

Crooks will be suspended for Hull's trip to Arsenal after receiving a yellow card against Ipswich at the weekend, while Cash will miss Villa's match at Manchester United after being booked for a foul against Fulham.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

Six other players are sitting on four bookings after nine rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (yellow card suspension)

Matty Cash - Aston Villa (yellow card suspension)

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Lisandro Martinez - Manchester United (red card suspension)

Omar Alderete - Sunderland (red card suspension)

#893. Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's  unfair trade practices.

In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.

Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.

Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."

China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."

Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.

Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.

Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.

German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.

Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.

In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.

"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."

Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:

"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.

According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.

While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.

The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.

Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."

Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.

Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.

Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.

Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.

MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.

This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.

"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

#892. Dazn secures exclusive deal on global streaming rights for 2029 Club World Cup

Deal deepens company’s relationship with Fifa

Dazn paid $1bn for global rights for the 2025 tournament

Dazn has secured an exclusive option for global streaming rights for the next men’s Club World Cup in 2029 in a development that deepens its partnership with Fifa.

The Saudi Arabia-backed ­streaming company came to Fifa’s aid before the inaugural 32-team Club World Cup in the US last year by agreeing to pay $1bn (£745m) for global rights for the tournament after many ­linear broadcasters and other streamers had declined to bid.

Apple TV had held talks with Fifa over a global streaming deal for 2025, but withdrew owing to a disagreement over valuation, and Fifa’s subsequent attempt to sell the rights on a regional basis foundered.

Dazn’s surprise late bid, facilitated by the purchase of a 10% stake in the company by Saudi’s Surj Sports Investment group, in effect bankrolled Fifa’s $1bn prize fund, with the winners, Chelsea, taking home about $114m (£85m).

Dazn is a loss-making business despite having more than 300 ­million registered users, with its 2025 accounts showing its operating losses increased from $772.9m to $939.8m over the previous 12 months, but appears content to continue to invest heavily in rights.

The value of its Club World Cup rights deal, or the point at which the option must be triggered, is not known but will give Fifa breathing space before the second edition of its expanded competition that has been designed as a major money ­spinner but remains fraught with political problems.

Planning for the 2029 tournament has proved difficult, with no decisions made on venues, format or size despite longstanding discussions between Fifa and the clubs about expanding to 48 teams, first reported by the Guardian two years ago.

Club World Cup progress has been a casualty of the fallout from Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off proposal, which led the lobby group European Football Clubs to threaten to withdraw its support. In a letter to Fifa obtained by the Guardian, EFC also expressed “serious concern and disappointment” at the delays in paying $250m in solidarity money owed to clubs from 2025 more than a year after the first competition had concluded.

Relations between EFC and Fifa are understood to have improved since the withdrawal of Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise plan, but they have yet to agree the finer details of a proposed joint venture to manage the Club World Cup’s commercial operations, which may be put on hold until after the Fifa presidential election in March.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The 2030 men’s World Cup co-host Morocco will be ­favourite to host in 2029 if Infantino is re-elected given his close relationship with King Mohammed VI.

Fifa’s decision to award hosting rights to the first women’s Club World Cup to the US, revealed by the Guardian last month, has strengthened Morocco’s case because the US was in the running for 2029.

A jointly-hosted tournament staged by Morocco and Spain is another possibility. Portugal, the third major 2030 co-host, is understood to have reservations about holding the event.
